extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society and learned natural philosophers (readers of 17th-century scientific reports)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for reporting and arguing about natural-philosophy observations, experiments, anatomical dissections, astronomical sightings, and mathematical demonstrations as exemplified in a 17th-century Philosophical Transactions issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require authentic testimony and further experiments for novel medical interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An authentic testimony is needed to undeceive the multitude about new medical operations; the author resolved to write no more on transfusion until some new experiments should countenance his first conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware malicious or false rumours; success on brutes does not suffice for confidence about humans; have persons of quality examine recovered patients to corroborate results; expect formal adjudication (e.g., by parliament or authoritative body) when controversy arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of injection experiments and anatomical drawings to demonstrate connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide drawings of organs (e.g., vasa deferentia and vesiculae seminales) as they appeared when cut out, and use injection experiments to demonstrate communications (e.g., that vesiculae seminales must be entirely filled before any liquor reaches the urethra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label figures clearly (letters denoting parts), report the experimental manipulation (where an injecting pipe was inserted, observed foramina, ducts), and use such direct manipulative evidence to support anatomical claims about pathways and communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical observations must record precise timing, position, trajectory, and comparative brightness
rubrics_metrics.description: Report dates/times and locations of observation; describe the path ('extended from the Whale through Eridanus'), apparent direction relative to the sun and horizon, apparent length in degrees, and relative magnitude/brightness (e.g., 'equal to the brightest of the fourth magnitude').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note atmospheric conditions (clouds, mists, horizon veiling), compare to prior recorded comets or catalogued stars, identify whether a nearby star is new by checking catalogues/globes/maps, and seek corroborating observations from other locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical exposition should present distinct stepwise reasoning and clear notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each distinct step of ratiocination or operation should have a separate line, with operations registered in the margin; use small letters for unknowns and capitals for knowns (as recommended in the described algebra translation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tables (e.g., of prime/incomposite numbers), many worked problems including those left obscure by earlier authors, and clear organization into propositions to enable students and readers to follow and verify methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: State limits when methods are non-geometrical (rule-and-compass criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations performed by means that are not by the sole aid of rule and compass should not be accounted geometrical (e.g., use of logistic/logarithmic curves for operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which constructions rely on additional curves or analytic methods and explain consequences (for example, why certain cubic equations cannot be solved by rule and compass alone).

rubrics_metrics.name: When applying geometric demonstrations to physical bodies, ensure requisite material conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical demonstrations applied to a physical body may fail if the requisite conditions of matter are not met; the defect of the conclusion should be judged according to the defect of matter from the requisite conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State axioms and conditions explicitly, note when idealized geometry does not capture physical imperfections, and temper theoretical conclusions with empirical qualification when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments must establish correct premises and correct computations
rubrics_metrics.description: A persuasive argumentative demonstration must correctly establish its minor and major premises and perform accurate computations (e.g., Angeli denies Riccioli's minor and demonstrates by computation that Riccioli's observation does not prove his claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check proportional reasoning (Rule-of-Three, proportions of distances/velocities), arithmetic used in geometric inferences, and consider alternative formulations of premises to avoid equivocation between apparent and real measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments with repetition, circumspection, and careful interpretation (control for compound motions/forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform experiments with due circumspection and multiple trials (e.g., Descartes's cannon discharged 24 times); interpret results considering composition of forces rather than leaping to single causal conclusions such as earth's motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report number of trials and outcomes, analyze possible compositions of motion/forces that could explain results, and avoid overinterpreting single or few runs—design to reveal or rule out alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assert novelty only after checking existing catalogues and prior observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Call a star 'new' only if it is not described in any catalogue, globe, or map; compare appearance and position with earlier comet observations (e.g., comet of 1664).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check with catalogs and prior records, document differences from previous events, and be cautious about transient visibility caused by atmospheric effects or horizon concealment.
